```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

Between 1900 and 1998 the leading causes of death in the United States
changed beyond recognition. Tuberculosis, the great killer of the early
century, almost disappeared; heart disease rose and then fell; cancer kept
climbing until the 1990s. A plot of the rates tells this story roughly.
Joinpoint regression tells it precisely: it finds the years in which a
trend changed direction or pace, and it summarizes each period by its
annual percent change (APC).

This vignette walks through a complete analysis with the `us_mortality`
data: age adjusted death rates per 100,000 for six causes.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
head(us_mortality)
```

## One series

Start with tuberculosis. `joinpoint()` takes the data, the time variable and
the response. By default it fits a log-linear model (so segments are
summarized by percent changes), searches for the best placement of 0 to
`kmax` joinpoints on the observed years, selects the number of joinpoints
with the weighted Bayesian information criterion (WBIC; Kim et al. 2023),
and computes empirical quantile confidence intervals (Kim et al. 2017).

```{r}
tb <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Tuberculosis")
fit_tb <- joinpoint(tb, x = year, y = rate, kmax = 3)
fit_tb
```

Three joinpoints split the century into four periods. The decline
accelerated from 3.7% per year to almost 15% per year after 1947, when
streptomycin came into use, and slowed again later. The asterisk marks APCs that
differ significantly from zero. The average annual percent change (AAPC)
condenses the whole century into one number.

The result tables are ordinary data frames:

```{r}
apc(fit_tb)[, c("start", "end", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value")]
joinpoints(fit_tb)
```

`autoplot()` draws the data, the fitted model, the joinpoints and the APC of
each segment. The shaded band is the 95% empirical quantile interval of the
fitted curve.

```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Tuberculosis death rate by year, 1900 to 1998, falling throughout, with the fitted model with three joinpoints, the APC of each segment, the 95% band of the fitted curve and gray bands for the confidence intervals of the joinpoint locations."}
autoplot(fit_tb, joinpoint_ci = TRUE)
```

The gray rectangles are the confidence intervals of the joinpoint
locations: the 1947 change is located within a few years.

## All causes at once

With `by`, each cause is fitted separately in one call.

```{r}
fit <- joinpoint(us_mortality, year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 3,
                 control = jp_control(aapc_last = 10))
```

Coloring segments by the direction of the trend turns the panel into a
summary of the epidemiological transition. On a logarithmic axis equal
percent changes look equally steep within a panel; the panels have their
own scales, so compare slopes across causes through their APCs.

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Six panels, one per cause of death, of age adjusted death rates on logarithmic axes, with the fitted segments colored by whether the trend significantly increased, significantly decreased or was stable."}
autoplot(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Age adjusted death rate per 100,000")
```

When the question is "how fast did each trend change, and when", the APC
plot reads more directly than the data. Each segment is drawn over the years
it covers, at the height of its APC, with its confidence interval as a band.

```{r, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Six panels showing, for each cause of death, the APC of every segment as a step over the years it covers, with confidence bands and a reference line at zero."}
plot_apc(fit)
```

AAPCs are best compared in a forest plot. The fit above requested the
last ten years in addition to the full range through
`jp_control(aapc_last = 10)`.

```{r, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "Forest plot of the average annual percent change of each cause of death over the full range and over the last ten years, with confidence intervals."}
plot_aapc(fit)
```

Over the century every cause but cancer and heart disease fell, but in the
last decade of the series cancer mortality was falling as well.

## Tables for a paper

`jp_table()` returns the trends formatted for a manuscript, with the
interval and p value of each estimate.

```{r}
knitr::kable(head(jp_table(fit, digits = 1), 8))
```

`model_estimates()` gives the regression coefficients (segment intercepts,
slopes and slope changes with their tests), and `model_selection()` the
statistics used to choose the number of joinpoints. `jp_export()` writes
every table to text files, one per table.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
jp_export(fit, "results", prefix = "mortality")
```

## Where to go next

- `vignette("published-analysis")` reproduces a published joinpoint analysis
  and its figures.
- `vignette("model-selection")` explains how the number of joinpoints is
  chosen and why methods disagree.
- `vignette("uncertainty")` covers error models, autocorrelation and the two
  kinds of confidence intervals.
- `vignette("comparing-groups")` tests whether two trends are parallel.
- `vignette("coding-changes")` handles outliers and changes in disease
  coding.
- `vignette("clustering")` finds age groups that share a trend.
- `vignette("extensions")` fits Poisson and logistic joinpoint models,
  adjusts for seasonality and estimates joinpoints between observations.
